div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

THE following epiqram on the fair sex was covered on an old window-pane: Nan can no more know woman's mind by tears Than by her shadow judge what clothes she wears. Farmer Brown: "This is the apiary." Cockney Visitor : "Is it, indeed? Where are the .pes ?" THE collar-stud has done more to release man from the tyranny of woman than all the philoso- phical works on humanity ever printed. AN optimist,is a man who Inuits on the bright side of everything, SO long as everything goes his

own way. Gus Tors "Poi'."—A carroty-headed man's pro- posal of marriage. TILE collars-worn in the i\liddlc Ages were ruff afrai re. When we say that a man is a brick we do not mean that he is taMnou clay. ASKED by his teacher the other day what he understood by an "unclean spirit," a, young Paddy promptly replied, "Plan yer honour, a

dhurty divi; l" • HONESTY i doubtless the best policy," says a waggish h. ue ace clerk ; "but it seems to have expired lols ago." THE man who has a long hair tangled in his coat button may pretend to be a misanthrope, but he can't deceive an), body. lureATiox may be the sincerest flattery ; but an up-to-date girl doesn't th nk so when she's pv,;• stilted with a paste diamoud "Mv dear doctor," said a lady, "1 uTer a great deal with my eyes." " Be patient, madam," replied he.; " you would probably snail- a great deal more without them." SUSPICION CONFID.3IZD.—MiS3 C3M4Ile : "I hear yon got married the other day." Mrs. De Koter "That's my business." Miss Caustic : "I thought so. This is your third, i-n't it ?" SHE AGREED. "I consider my judgment infinitely superior to yours," said Mr. 'noggins to his wife, after a long and terrible dispute. " agree with you, thoroughly," returned the lady. Muggings stared. "Yes," she continued. "I mean when you asked me to marry You, and I was fool enough to consent." Fiusr NEIGHBOUR "1 ray, it's too had! Your dog has been worrying my eat !" Second Neigh- bour : "Serve it right;! Your cat has ben worrying me every night for the last six months I" MOLE CERTAIN.—Jack: "So you knew I loved you?" Ada: "Yes, I have known it for some time." Jack : "Au, what was it told you—your womanly intuition?" Ada: "No; your sister Jennie.' A SIMPLE REMEDY.—Mother: " Ah, doctor, my son is so poorly and jaded, he never gets to sleep before three o'clock. Cannot you do some- thing for him " 'Doctor: " Hum ; Suppose we try a simple remedy to start with; let us make him give up his latchkey 1" A Runt OF BUSINESS.—III a grocer's shop, about a quarter pas eight the other morning, the shopmen were gossiping, when a small boy entered: Twa fardens for a ha'penny, please." "Coats off, gentlemen; business has begun I" cried the manager. Too DASHFUL.—" Is anybody waiting on you?" said a polite salesman to a young lady from the country. "Yes, air," replied the blushing dam- sel ; "that's my young man outside—he wouldn't come into the shop." A CANDID SPINSTER.—Miss Dalrymple sister of Lord FLiles, was somewhat deformed, while amiable and judicious above the average of he: sex. Taking into view her beautiful place of resi- dence and her large wealth, she remarked to a friend one day, "I can say, for the honour of man, that I never got an offer in my life." IT OFTEN WORKS THAT WAY.—,-MPS. WaybaCk "Young Jim Junkett don't seem to amoutl . to much since he left college." Mr. Waybe.ek "No. You see his college education made him too smart to work, and not smart enough to get along without work." PARSON: "I was glad to see, farmer, that your attention was so fixed on me when I was preac..ing this morning." Farmer: "Yea, parson. I was trying' to make out what on earth you was drivin' at. 1 be a man that alias likei to get at the bottom of a thing, but you lioked me this mornin', parson ! " TIIE FAVOURITE TOPIC.—TaIk to woman about religion, she sighs; talk to her of love, she simpers; talk to her of art, he yawns ; talk to her of science, she goes to seep ; but talk to her of dress, and she will open her eyes, and give you the entire attention of her ears. HE KNEw.—Teacher (impressing one of her protepis : "Be brave and earnest and you will succeed. Do you remember my telling you of the great difficulty George Washington had to contend with?" Willy Raggs : "Yes, mum ; he couldn't tell a lie 1" A FATAL MisTaks.—Henderson : "You say you are broke. Ask your friend Collins to lend you a few shillings." Williamson: "It'. no use. The other day he told several of us fellows a joke, and I forgot to laugh." MAGISTRATE—" It's very disgraceful that you should beat your wife." Prisoner—" Well, your Worship, she aggrawated me by keepin' on Ba y n' she'd 'aye me hUp nolo that bald-'eaded hold 'urn- bug, mean in' yer Worship." Magistrate—" You're discharged." ETHICS VERSUS ..X.STHETICS.—She (with convic- tion) : "I don't believe in cutting up -poor little birds and putting them on hats." He: Oh, how good you are I" She: "Its so much prettier to use the whole bird." • CONJUGAL AGREHMENT.—Mrs, Bicker (petu- lantly) : "Oh, it's all very well to talk, but you'd be glad if I were dead!" Mr. Picker (blandly): "Whatever you do, dear, is sure to be the right LADY OF THE HOUSE—" During the last week -you have had three different policemen visiting you. I don't propose to put up with any such conduct." New Cook—" It's not my fault. The bill of fare in this house is so poor that no police. man can stand it more than two days. div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

MY DEATtEST NELLIE, The cold weather has come now in earnest, and there is no use thinking yet of lighter costumes. A cosy and serviceable paletot for a girl from boar to nine years is made ni h a double detachable cape Which enables either the paletot or the cape alone to be worn separately when the milder weather comes. The material ie green visrmamr camel heir, trimmed with beaver, or, for little children, grey, blue, fawn, or pink eieth, trireme," with white hAre, wPuld lo&:ery pretty, Led jar the v.(fier girls thrk-colouici cloth or serge, trimmed with astraelian, might I e f,ubstittlted for the camel- hair and beawr,'and a large, srti,3lo hat, made of the same material, should take the plans ef the hood in g'rls over ii yews old. , Another very pretty Valtot is made with a bez- pleat front and baele, end the new eqUare shoulder pieces of velvet !nun% 17cernbling a large sailor co'iar, which will be a distinct feature of the spring fashions, both far the little folks and their Wen. The circular shoulder cape is with the "sailor" collar, detachable, and can is, worn later on as a light „school wrap, without the warmer paletot. Liberty's thick camel-hair is one of the nicest materials I know for children's winter wear; it is SO soft, warm, and light. Nevertheless, little girls of the " tomboy " persuasion should be attired in something snore substantial; good wiry diagonal serge, which will resist even the onslaught of brambles and fence nails.

I have seen a great many neutral coloured felt) bats, and several of them are very pretty at this time of the year. I noticed one in silver grey in a sailor shape, the brim was bound with two rolls of black velvet, and the crown trimmed with a velvet bow, olasped in front with a paste buckle, a little tuft of violets was placed on either side of the front with a green osprey rising out of the centre of the one on the left. Bonnets are now so mall, and require such a little trimming, that it does not rEquire much skill to turn out a really pretty bonnet at home; small Dutch shapes are usually becoming, these have an Aleatia.n bow in front with a bunch of fl mere at the back of the crown, a black osprey should he attached amongst the blossoms to relieve the flit effect. An attractive one was somewhat of the Alpine shape, trimmed with ribbon and An erect aigrette ot cock's feathers and a white osprey. The same deign as this looks very well, too, when bound with astrachan.

In indoor costumes the round-waisted bodices are still almost universally worn, but it must be confessed that they do not suit every figure, and some women still prefer to wear the graceful pointed bodices, which invariably look neat and trim, and improve the contour of waist and hips. A very pretty bodice is of figured ort pon or silk, slightly fulled on to the velvet yoke in front, and shaped into aeh Arp point. The yoke is outlined with jet or gimp, and the velvet neck- band is finished with two chmx rosettes of ribbon at the sides. The bodice lining must be made to fasten straight down the front in the ordinary fashion, and the yoke and full portion must be hooked over neatly. Heliotrope or pale alue figured material, with dark-green velvet, would be a nice combination of colour for a smart dress, but care must be taken to secure just the right tints. Some colour combinations that sound b zlrre are often really harmonious, while others are the reverse, simply because a mistake has been made in the selection of one or the other.

Muth are growing large,- and m,re obtrusively frilled and ornomenteil T P latest have brighb coloured silk ft ,unces spre sing 0 .tworcle from the centre and tied with green ribbons in which bunches of violets ususl y nestle. Tido combina- tion of violets and green rilPlons may be a'most sail to be unive-s 1, but it is o%sionally displaced by pink poppies with block ve, v., centres, tied up with black satin ribbons ; or small dahlias in their varied tints. A charming model was made of delicate peach blossom velvet edged with a satin bouillonto in keeping, and headed with a huge double-looped bow in emerald-green velvet, orna- mented with humming-birds. Yours lovingly, JEissan.

Mrs. Vanderbiltis a wont in of trirnte than average tact and abili7y. She is not what would gener,lly termed pretty, says the tt Westminster Gsz-4. te," but notwithstanding that she lias grown ehithen, she has a slight, ,almost girlish figure, and a very winning and captivating ma miler. Not one piece of jewellery is ever seen upon her in. the street or in the broad day light,and a glance at the quietly-dressed woman who rolls past in her carriage, would not suggest that she was the wife of the richest man in America ' and had four or five goodly fortunes locked nu in tier jewel-caskets.

• A Good Husband and How to Choose Him. As a husband the man with a hobby is hard to heat. The amatuer carpenter, the lover of -Lowers. the bud• ding photographer, the proud poFsessor of a lathe, and the home artist, have each and everyone qualities which qualities which go far to convert a house into a home. The man who potters about the house with a hammer and a saw, and who, periaos, perpetrates atrocities in the way of bookcases and executes fearful and wonder- ful daubs upon the door panels, or who may delight in the creation of zoological curiosities in fretwork nearly sure to be a good fallow and a good husband. What if he does mend the chair leg or atfix the sofa castor with the air of a man designing a castle or a bridge ? It keens him out of mischief. To those girls who are in the fortunate position of being :dole to pick and choose, no better advice can be given than to marry a man with a hobby. 'rhe lover of books is certainly entitled to talc,. high rank on the list 'ii good hushands. Fix him indlis favourite arm-chair, give bird his favourite author, and wild horses won't stir him. If he has a fault, it is that he is somewhat taci- t irn, and does not find the weather such an absorbing t pie, of conversation as the wife of I;j bi mom would a iiwitimes like. Still, he finds his paradise at his own firesite, and the pipe he smokes is the, pipe of peace. Finally, the youth who has been brought up with a large family of brothers and sisters may be commended for marital honours. The ethic; of giving and taking, which may be termed the A B C of domestic felicity, have been impressed upon him by his home life, and he understands the meaning of self-sacrifice. All of the qualincations given are tolerably' sure to develop a good husband. But girls should not forget that much of their wedded happiness will depend upon themselves. The good husband of to-day may become the bad one of to-morrow, made so by an unwM3 or unworthy wife.

Far down beneath this letter'd stone A friend belov'd we laid ; To blend with dust, and dust alone, Wrapp'd in eternal shade. And still our hearts are sad and sore, . Our rears wilt not refrain ; For we shall see his lace no more, Is.for hear his voice again. The morn to him will ne'er unfold Her stores of and joy ; Nor lovely sunset, Rusted with gold, Again his thoughts employ. Upon his grave the stars of night Will shine when heaven is clear ; But never will their kindly light Within that grave appear.

The songs of spring, the summer flowers, Mild autumn's balmy breath ; And icy winter's storms and showers Reach not the land of death. And all in vain are sorrow's wail And pleading voice ol prayer ; To pierce the grave's eternal vail, . Or wake the sleeper there. The days and years will come and go, Life's tide incessant roll ; And scenes of labour, mirth, and woe, Absorb each living soul : But all unconscious lie the dead lu Sheol's solitude ; Where liviag foot my never tread, Nor living voice intrude. Seen through the mist of human tears. The grave is darkness all ; And while we gaze our hopes and fears Alternate rise and fall. The breath of spring new life can give, And flowers that died will bloom ; But sa ,can dust and ashes live, Can life spring from the tomb Is there some germ that lies conceard Within its dark recess ; Some body yet to he reveard From out its nothingness ?

It may be so : but from her graves Ztrth sends us no reply ; And all the dead beneath the waves In squat silence lie. Yet hope still lingers o'er the scene And bids our fears subside ; Lives not the wondrous Nazarene Who for our ransom died! His power, that from a mountain grave Itecall'd a friend beloy'd ; Is still omnipotent to save, Is still with pity moved. . And 0, when dawns the glorious morn For which Creation sighs ; The dead in Him, poor mortals born, Will then immortal rise. J. H. W. CLINDINNINCI.

div.p: WE PARTED AT THE ALTAR;
BY LAURA JEAN LIBBEY,
Author of "A Mad netrathal," "lone," "Park by Fate," "Floribers Lover," etc., etc. ,
CHAPTER M.

will turn you from her door for this" "Oh, yes, yes," sobbed Doris. "I am as sure of it as though it had already happened." As she speaks a strange thought flits through his brain—a thought that twenty-four hours ago he would have scouted. "Oh, what slfall I do, Mr. Frederick r she moaned. "I am so young—l—l am afraid of the great, gold, cruel world." "You shall not face the cruel world, Doris," he said, huskily. • "I am a gentleman. I cannot leave you in distress brought on by myself. There ;is but one way out of the difficulty, and that is this: I must marry you." "Marry me 1" she echoes, her little hands drops ping from her tear-stained eyes, and gazing at him aghast. "Do you see any other way out of it ?" he asks, repressing a groan tint rose to his lips. "I con- fess that I do• not, under the circumstances. I • ;must make the only atonement possible. I must make you my wife, if you ,are 'willing. It i the only reparation within my power. Will you accept .it, poor little Doris ?" She.lookecl,np at .him wistfully. "Do.you really want me to marry you ?" she tt,lted, shyly and wonderingly. "I suppose that would be the only proper thing," lie remarked, hopelessly. "But do people ever marry each other who have only been acquainted such a short while as we have keen—not quite a week ?" "Sometimes," he answered, abstractedly. "How strange it is that you should really want to marry me," she mused. don't see what for. But, really, I don't mind if—if you want me so very much " Want her I He could have laugh° if aloud at the very idea. He did not want her. He was forced, as it were, into making her his wife. He could have Cursed his folly, as he stood there, that had led him into the fatal error that had persuaded her in- to goinr to that ball. He aroused himself from his bitter thoughts by a great effort. • "It may.as well be now, Doris," he said, with reckless despair. "No doubt we can find some- body to perform the ceremony at once." She was mantic and impressible. Ah ! how nice it would be to have a handsome young hus- band like Frederick Thornton to love end protect her. There would be no bitter scoldiNgs and harsh, grim Madame Delm,ar ; no more heartaches because she was alone in the great, cold world. She had led such alonely life; her poor heart had always • craved love so much. She never forgot that ride through the sweet, pink clover to the stone church that stood on the cliff overlooking the glittering Chesapeake. How , the night-birds twittered, and the crickets chirped, and the fireflies twinkled like earth-stars in the green grass by the roadside. She had a dim recollection of the few moments that were spent in the oil rector's parlour, and of how the rectors daughter had lent her her own wedding veil to wear, and of Frederick leading her' up the dint aisle of the church—up to the altar—his face grave almost to sternness, and pale as death. Oh I how weird it all seemed to Doris. Then, as if in a dream, she stood quite still by his side while the fatal ceremony went on. She heard the questions and responses and answered the ques- tions put to her; and the white-haired minister pronounced ;her his lawful wedded wife. The bridegroom bent down his handsome head to kiss h s bride; he knew it was customary, it was expected of him. Doris drew back with a startled cry, for his lips were as cold as ice. Poor little bride! It was done. In a moment she had sown the seeds from which Was to spring up a harvest of woe so terrible that her wildest imagination could never have painted it. "Are you glad to have married me, Mr. Freder- ick ? " she whispered, timidly, as they turned from the dim old altar towards the vestry to sign the register. "Glad 1" he groaned, under his breath. But low as the words were muttered, her strained ear caught them, and every word shocked her, and stabbed her heart like the thrust of a dagger. " Glad I You have wrecked my life. You have parted me" for ever from Vivian, whom I loved so madly, I have given you my name. I. will care for you, because in the eyes of the world you are My wife; but here at the altar we part. I pray Heaven I may never look on your face again." . She did not faint. She did not cry out, or utter any moan. All in a moment her young heart seemed turned to stone. When the names were all signed in the register, Doris turned piteously to her bridegroom: "I have one prayer to make," she said. "All— even you, Frederick—leowe me alone in the vestry for a brief 'half hour. Do not refuse me. ,You will come here alone to m then, Frederick, my husband." It was a strange, unheard-of request. He bowed wonderingly, and left her, and the door closed after him, shutting him out from her view. "He married me- and he does not love me l" she moaned, wildly, as she sank &um shivering on her knees. "I have wrecked his life, for I have parted hint from Vivian. That is what he said. Oh, I heard it. But it is not too late to repair what I have done." she panted, as the low dash of the waves caught her ear. "I can set him free at.the very altar. I can, and I will. If I have to part from hum, I had better die." And this brings us back, dear reader, to the pitiful scene that opens this story.

MARRYING IN HASTE. WHEN Doris entered the grand ball-room she 'caught her breath with a cry of delight. "Oh, Mr. Freilei ick She grasped, clutching at his arm with lei' little, trembling white hands, it seems like fairyland--ora - a glinipse ot heaven !" Frederii k Thornton laughed amusedly ; to him there was nothing out of the common in the banks. of roses; the palm, aod waving ferns, the dazzling 'chandeliers, and the unique and brilliant costume of bewitchingly pretty maidens'and passg matrons. "A young. girl's first ball does. seem like a glimpse of fairy life," he answered, gaily. "Those that follow never seem quite so nice." "I shall always remetnhr you when I think of My first ban," she answered, impulsively. "And, 'indeed, I am qinte sure it Will be my last and only one 'No one will ever take me to a ball again." "Do not be so sure of that, Doris," he replied, in a low voice. "What are you thinking of that you gaze so intently on that bank of roses ?" he asked, Curiously. "I w .s thinking what' a pity it was to cut them from the stem and bring them here, for just a few hours. By to-morrow they will all lie withered and dead against that wall." "What a waste of pity !" he laughed: "They' will have served their purpose well--gladdened the eye, delighted the sense. But come; the band is about to strike, up a waltz. I hope you have learned to waltz, Doris." The hour that followed seemed like a dream to peioloia.,miii{rietttye lliitgto hltslor a)ndisiheSnl:ue could have ever danced and for ever. And in the excitement, the revelry, the brilliancy, can be wondered that time seemed fairly to take wings and whirl away ? Dorisid _EA been very much abashed at first to see that she was, as usual, the poorest dressed girl in the gay throng; but in the excitement of the lights and music, and in the exuberance of happy youth, site soon forgot it, and was enjoying herself as she had never enjoyed het self i efore. The eyes of the gentlemen followed her adrdr- ingly, and the ;adios, in Consequence, were exceed- ingly jealous and envious. " Who is she ?" they asked of each other. But nobody seenied!to know, • . - -.4, In all her simpleness and plainness, as is tften the ease, even ainidst that throng of beauties, Doris was acknowledged the belle of the grand ball. Mrs. Langilon. the hostess, gazed at the pretty young girl in wonder, and at last she sought her son. "Max," she said, leading him aside, "who is that young girl? How ca.lie she here? Who in- vited her?" "I did, mother," he responded, promptly. "She is one of the seminary girls. Miss Doris Brandon is her name, I believe. You remember we sent a card to Miss Courtney. She could sot attend. And my old chum there, Frederick Thornton, asked me to send a card to her, and, of course, I complied. Are you displeased, mother?" "No," she answered. "Still, I should have b en Vetter 'pleased had I been co ,sulted first. The girl is pretty, I grant you; but she does not look quite at hems in our set, and you know how particular I am in that regard." "She may be a little awkward," laughed the son. " School-gi, Is have the reputation for being so. She must be our equal socially some millionaire's daughter—or Thornton would not be paying so much attention to her. He never takes a step backward in the social scale, you know." Mrs. Langton looked relieved. On returning to the ball-room she observed that young Mr. Thornton and the pretty belle of the ball had dis- appeared. As we have said, time flew by on golden wings. Neither Doris nor Frederick noted the fleeting moments. , Over and over again Doris told herself how happy she was as she looked into Frederick Thorn- ton s handsome face with glad, shining eyes. In those blissful moments, a woman s heritage of love had come to her and more than once that evening the thou 'lit occurred that her life would be doubly dark aml dreary when lie left the village. She dared xiot think of the cold, dark hours when she sh!iuld see him no more. And like the faint echo of a dream, the words of the poet returned to her: "Perchance if we had never met I had been spared this vain regret; And yet I could not bear the pain Of never seeing thee again." "Yes, Doris had learned ato love him—love him with all the deep, romantic passion of her girlish• heart. With youth, love is not a plant of slow growth, The glance of an eye, the tench of a hand, a smile. a tender word, often lights the flame of a deathless love. In striving to be kind to Doris, to make this ball a happy. metnora.ble epoch in her girlish life, Frederick Thornton had unwittingly opened her eyes to the truth. She was deeply in love, with him. But, girl-like, she would have died rather than he should guess her sweet secret. Suddenly he paused abruptly, in the midst of a waltz. "I am afraid it is almost time to go, Doris," he said, hurriedly taking out his watch and glancing at it. Great Heaven ! was he mad or dreaming? It wanted exactly eight minutes to half-past ten—the time for closing the seminary gates. • "Doris," he said gently. She turne 1 a startled ace toward him. ' "Oh. Mr. Frederick, what is it? Why do you look like that? 'What, is the matter?" "We must go at once, Doris," he said. ." We have not a moment to lose. We have not seven minutes left to reach the seminary. It wants just that time to half-past ten." , He never forgot the deadly, awful despair that came over her face—the ghastly pallor—how the blue eyes darkened with awful fear. "Oh, Mr. Frederick 1" she gasped. "What shall I do ? " "Courage, Doris," he said. "We can make it U you are quick 'in getting your wraps." A moment more and they were out in the star- light together, fairly flying down the white road. Be could barely keep pace with the girl's fleet footsteps. She was out of breath as they reached the steep path that led up the rugged hillside to the semi- nary, and was obliged to take his arm. More and more deadly grew her fear as moment after moment slipped by. Frederick Thornton could hear the quick beating of the girls heart and the piteous sighs that shook her slender frame. "Doris, are you crying?" he suddenly asked, in deep distress. • Before she could reply, from a church tower near them the hour of eleven rang out, slow, solemn strokes, each one a death-knell to Doris. She fell clown on her knees in the path, unable to move a step further, sobbing as he had never heard any ono sob in his life before Ah 1 the pity of it I His watch w is half an hour late. He could see the great, heavy iron gate from where he stood. The gate aaa closed. "Oh, Mr. Frederick! Mr. Fr.,:.eriek l what shall I do?" moaned Doris. "Madame will never let me enter her door again. Oh, I am lost I lost lost! lam homeless, penniless ! I will be thrown on the world's mercy, with nowhere to go It was my only refuge, and now I have lost ill Oh, if I could but die !" Frederick Thornton stood before the kneeling little figure like one petrified. "I will take al tile blame upon myself, Doris," he said, huskily, "for assuredly the fault was mine in coaxing you to go. Come, cheer up. Ail will be well. ome, let us walk boldly up to the gate and ring the bell." Doris drew back iq terror too great for words. "It would make matters no better. You do not know madame. She will never let me enter her door again. Oh, I wish I were dead i" "I meant that you should have such a happy time in going to the ball," he said, gently. "I am so sorry it has ended so." . She bowed her beautiful golden head Until it touched the cold stones. " Where can I go? What shall I do, Mr. Frederick ?" she sobbed. "I am so young and friendless ! 011, I wish that I had died when I was so happy amidst the lights and the music, dancing with you at the ball l" She was clinging to him like a terrified child, sobbing piteously now. He was quite at a loss what to say to comfort her. "Are you quite sure it will be as bad as you say, Doris r' he asked. hoarsely. "Are you sure she

TiE clock in the church tower struck the mita- night hour in slow, measured strokes, and Doris struggled up from her knees with a wild panting cry, sobbing out: When he returns he must not find me here." Then in her bridal robes, without one backward glance, she stole from the vestry out into the cold, moonlit night. The terrible revelation, as they turned away from the very altar, that her bridegroom had not married her for love, had almost turned poor Doris's brain; and her one mad thought was to set him free again, by seeking rest in the dark, cold water, and end it all. , Hurrying down the path, without one glance behind at the dimly-lighted old church, and the coach with the restless white horses standing • before its door, she reached the brink of the bay, tipped by the golden, arrowy light of the stars. Tee tide was coming in. The water was rising higher and higher each moment, with the waver- ing moon-track across it. It would soon reach the rock where she stood, and sweep her away. "No one cares what becomes of me," sobbed Doris, piteously. " What have I done that I should be so miserable and friendless? Life would have been so different if Frederick could only have loved .me. Oh, •it is so cruel, cruel I H even forgive me!" she cried. "I am so lonely, so desolate!' • "Doris l'' The sound of her own name startled her so she would have fallen backward from the rock on which she was standing, down into the seething water below, if a strong arm had not ben put out , hurriedly and caught her ,` 'mid, turning her white, terrified face, Doris found herself confronted by Frederick Thornton. .

" Doris !" he repeated, in amazement, "what are you doing here? You requested me to leave you half an hour by yourself in the vestry. I came down to the bay to while away the time. How is it 1 find you here?" As he spoke be looked keenly, curiously into the fair young lace, which was flushing and paling so piteously. • He was quick to notice the great change in her —how she shrank from his outstretched hand, and how her eyes drooped before his steady gaze . In a flash t occurred to Doris that he had not been to the vestry, and he had not read the note she had left there addressed to him. S he did not know what bad brought her to the dark, restless waters of the bay ; a d, standing face to face with him, she could not tell him. " This is the height of imprudence, little Doris," he said, taking her hand, and drawing it through h a arm. "Surely, Doris, you do not repent our hasty marriage, do you ?" he asked suddenly ; and he was greatly troubled lait dismayed to see her nod her curly lies land burst; in o tears. Put on your wraps quickly. V. must catch the 1.20 train, and we have quite a long ride before us." He had spoken so gently, so kindly to her, a great throbbing hope suddenly sprang to life in Doris's heart. He had married her without love ; but pet imps, in the time to come' she might win that love, if she did not part frornhim at the

I should be awkward and ill at ease before them; I should not know what to do, what to say, or how to say it. I, who have been a poor, little, dependent nobody all my life, know nothing of your world and its way, and you would be ashamed of me. You would repent marrying me, and I should die," she moaned, under her breath. , "My bother and sisters are by no means formid- able persons," he said, frowning slightly. "They are well-bred, a trifle haufhty perhaps (all save one of them), dainty and refined. They are ladies 'whom it will be a pleasure for you to meet." "Tell me more of them," said Doris, faintly, her courage sinking lower and ' lower at every word he uttered. Oh I how she dreaded to meet his relatives " I will begin with my mother," he eaid, "and sketch really faithful portraits for you: She has more pride and dignity, we think, than any other member of the faintly. She is tall and stately; her eyes are clear, cold and gray. She is the very embodiment of the term, a well-bred, haughty lady." "And your sisters—are they like your mother ?" faltered Doris, still more faintly. " I.have three sisters," he responded. "Isabel, the eldest, is very like mother in face and manner; Gweridolin is called the blonde beauty of the family, and Beatrix, or Prizy, as we always call her—welt, I can hardly find words to tell you 'what she is like. She is, I must confess, a great cross to my dignified mother. She is sixteen, and the romp, the tomboy, the mischievous sprite of the family. She has very expressive eyes, brown and sparkling, but she can never be What is called good-looking, for her hair is positively red. My father is a stately gsntleman, bound up in his business cares. What lam you can see for your- self. I think I have given you a fair picture of the inmates of Thornton Villa, as our home is called " As Doris listened the presentiment grew stronger and stronger that every one in this stately home would be antagonistic to herself. "And your mother being what she is, so haughty and proud, wished you to marl y some one like herself, no doubt," said Doris, in a low voice. • "Yes," replied Frederick Thornton, huskily. "My mother wished me to marry Vivian Court- ney,' and he uttered a deep sigh. , Doris crept closer to him, looking breathlessly up into his face with her great, blue, shining eyes. "Tell me—if it had not been for me—for taking me to the fatal ball, which ended so fatefully— tell me, would you have married Vivian ?" He was too honourable and straightforward to deceive her. He bowed his head. "It would, have been so, Doris," he answered huskily. "You loved her so well," she whispered below her breath, her face growing paler and paler; but he did not notice that. "Yes," he replied, but added, hastily: "why talk of that, now! It is all over between Vivian and me." "I have' come between you and the girl you loved," breathed Doris. "Let use forget if I can," he cried out sharply. "'Don't torture in, by reminding me of what might have been." Then he relapsed into silence again, and his face, half averted from her, grew sterner, colder, and prouder than ever. He did not notice how wistful was the fair young face turned to him. He was ill at ease; he had found the wedding journey decidedly irksome; he longed to be away from her; and thus two hours dragged wearily by, and the palace coach with its ill-mated bride and groom, whirled on through the darkness. . She clinched her liWe hand; she tried to still the beating of her heart He was solicitous for her comfort, he was attentive to her wants, but she noticed after that allusion which awakened his remem ranee of Vivian, his lost love, that he spoke to her only when civility dictated that he should speak; and 'When he did address her he never looked at her. From her, heart she longed to be back with Madame Darnel' again.- 'Ali I was ever a bride so lonely before? Did any young girl ever meet such a strange fate as this? Sitting there by her young ;,usband's side, so cruelly, bitterly unhappy, on her , 'wedding journey, the words of an old poem came to her, tilling her eyes with tears: 'Like some divided river, Your ways and mine will be. To drift apart forever— Forever till the sea." (lo be continued).

He -Ins written fifty books is deeply versed in . Inedissval myths and legends, and at the same time is in sympathy with modern life and progress. The proposal to extenti the borough of Warring- ton has met with various roceptions at the bands of the di-rent townships affected thereby. Little Sankey, which is to be swaliowed up entirely, has consented to go into the borough. considering the terms offered as beneficial. Latchford Without has adopted the same course. A piece of Poulton-with- Fearahead is asked for, in order to straighten the borough boundary, which is of a peculiar shap,- just in that spot, but the Parish Council of the town- ship does not see its way to give thisliece up and are determined if possible to be "wedged" into the borough. The greatest opposition to the exten.ion tiewever, comes from Appleton, arlrich embraces Stockton Heath. A formidable list, (3f objections has been drawn ,np, and the Parish 'Council is evi- dently going to do its utmost to oppese the exten- tion in this direction. They consider • that the .change will be to the advantage of Warrington in; , ^every respect and not ot the slighte.sit advantage tol Appleton. The borough, •however, will naturally r extend in that direction towards the Ship Canal,' sr and no doubt this fact will be considered when tke inquiry is held, and will have ,great weight int favour of Warrington.

The river Nlersey pre,tents a very unusual appear- ance in consequence of the continued frost. The high tideti have prevented the river from being frozen over in a compact mass, but its course is almost blocked by.pieces of ice of all sizes which extend from one side of the river to the other. Immediately below the .weir, the foam is frozen and it almost has the appearance of soap suds. The weather hits however not been so severe in 'War- rington this year as it was in ganuary 1881, for in that year, hundreds of Warringtonians disported themselves upon tie river, which was frozen over from'Fiddlers'Verry almost to its source. The cold did not continue so long that 'ear, but it was ex- ceptionally severe while it lasted.

The weather last .week 'has been unusually cold, and accompanied with it at times has been a curt,ng wind, which caused the greatest discom- fort. The effect upon the town has been marked indeed, for instead of the stzeets being crowded in the evenings. they present a deserted appearance. Instead of "trashing" in the streets, otrr young people are " keeping the the warm," and the same applies to the older and more staid members of the Community. It is not pleasant to promenade the streets in about 14 or 16 degrees of frost, and no one does So unless it is a matter of duty or neces- sity. There is now a grand chance of grucluating for Arctic explorers, but' there are apparently very few whose ambitions lie in this direction.

There are, however, a number, and a large num- ber too, who are putting in full time on the ice, pf ich there is more than there has usually been about Warringrou'dnring-the winter. The skaters ve had no re vein to grutottle for want of opportu- tmity to indaigi in theit'favourite *title. Since the present yeareame in,.they have prac•ically had. the field to thernsolves.for there have only hen one .or two angle, thaws. ,',Very rarely does it happen in tilligland that there are six weeks' qmost continuous •shatinz, and we are fast becoming accustomed to this hyperborean state of things. There is however a dark side to all this. The -severe weather has thrown a large number of peole-Outrof work, and the distress at .pres.nt is 'probably egual to that caused by the coal -strike. It is satisfactory to note that the Relief 'Committee has beeu expending the fund left over from last year, in relieving tho ',distress, and that a soup kitchen has been opened at the Drill Hall. No doubt this will do a great deal towards relieving the worst•cases, hut for itll this, the'!stifferings of some of the poor people Laust be terrible.

1 I am gltd to notice that some of the fortunate 4.41 ' •tilluale who have ,flooded their fields-forprovid- lug skatinke-with enjlyraent and thereby reaping a golden harvest are giving of their plenty. Mr. Newa ton, of the Twi,gery farm, Manchester-road, has- especially distinguished himself in this respect,and_ no less a sum than £l9 has beesi,handed over to the Infirmary, and .£2l to- the unenioloyed.fund. div.head: TEE DISTRESS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: TEE DISTRESS AT WAR- RINGTON.
THE VNEMPLOY,ED AND TBE CORPORATION:

Several meetings of the unemptoyed have been held during the 'past week, and on Thursday morning a- boyt 500 of them met at Bridge Foot, where Mr. John Price addressed them. He urged them te show the auth- orities that they did not mean to atarve,and be denounc- ed in strong language, what he termed the " hole and corner " method of distributing tickets for relief. He said that the. Corporation should either find food or work fer the. unemployed, and that the Town Clerk should call a meeting upon the suhject. He had been given to undeistaintrhist a pr. icgssiou to the Town Hall would not be allovied; and therefore, he called upon all pre,ent to walk in a batty to the place in order to show that they were in earnest in their desire that the Cor— poration should bestir themselves in the matter. The men then formed in procesesino and marched in a body to the front of the Town I Alter waiting here for some time, a deputation- ' o#l*.'proeeeded to the , Town Clerk's office, where the.V.lrtre met by Mr. J. ' Leon Whittle (rownCleik), Mr.StanfeyWillon (Deputy- Town Clerk, and Secreiary of the Relief Committee), and Mr. T. Longdin (borough surveyor). The leader of the deputation stated that they represented the unemployed of the town, and had come tge know what the Corporation were prepared to da RP them during the present severe weather. He said that many of the men were starving, and that it was high time that something was done. He then read two re- sclutions which had been passed a .the meeting at Bridge Foot. The first skthat thl ney which was it 6 left over from last year 'e ' ief fun uld be a". once ! utilized for the present diamts. 6 second was that work should be found for as many 'as possible of the unemployed. In repiny to the first resolution, Mr. Whittle and Mr. Wilson inkrmed the deputation that the Relief Committee had already relieved numerous cases of , poverty, and that they had already decided to opm a ' soup kitchen on ;Friday. Mr. Longdin, in re- ply to the seconfd resolution, said that it was an ' utter impos ility to. find work outside, owing to the severe s te of the weather. All the Cor- poration work was at standstill, but the men in its ..i. employ were being keptori: The Town Clerk further informed the deputation'thatiOwas not the duty of the Corporation to find work for the unemplbYel„ but they were always willing to fin them work if it were possible. Had the weather perthit it, many streets would he pulled up, and paved, but i as impossible to do this work at present. He also reminded them that last year, during tb..., ~..,..al strike, an expenditure, of almost £2,000 was made to find work for the unemployed,and that was now a charge upon the rates, which they were now having to pay. He would like to hear any suggestions which the deputation had to make upon the subject. The members of the d. potation however, stated that after what had been said, they were satisii-d that no work could be feund, and wished to be informed of the arrangements for the distribution of relief. Mr. Whittle told them that they could have tickets at Bank House, authorising them to obtain the soup and bread. The deputation informed the Town Clerk thatgreat dissatis- faction was expres.sed at the conduct of Mr. Byrne, the visiting officer because of his unsympathetic , manner, and also because he was an army pensioner. The Town Clerk said that two police officers would be ' in attendance at.the distribution of tickets. The depute- ' 'tient then w:thdrew.

Upon coming out-ef the Town Hall, they informed Mr. Price of the result of their interview, after which the latter harangued the people from the Town Hall steps. Fle said that the whole interview was most unsatisfac- tory, and that the Town Clerk had not treated the un- employed as he ought to have done. He wanted to know what was going to bo done on Sunday as well as week , days. He also complained that no member of the Town , Council was present at the interview. They wet • ex- pecting the Mayor at the Town Hall in a short time, and he advised the mon to wait until he arrived, and try to get satisfaction from him. He asked those in favour of stopping until the Mayor came, to put no two hands. It was decided to await the arrival of his Worship. As the afternoon was bi tarty c Id. ne men went la a body to the DrIJI Hall. and took possession of it before the occupantswere aware of their 'coming, arid an im- promptu meeting was held. Mr. Price launched forth in bitter denu,clation of capitalists And all of that ilk. The leader of the deputation to the Town Clerk also denounced the Corporation ”fficials.

After some time, it was diicov-ered thlt the Mayor had arrived, and the procession carre back in front of the Town Hall. After waiting here about a quarter of an I 1 hour. Inspector Spinks asked for two genuine Warring- ton men to form a deputation to the Mayor and the ' Watch Committee. Two men then proceeded to the Icommittee room, and were informed of the result of th- meeting of the relief committee that morning. After , they haAtinformed their companions below, Inspector Spinks coming to the Town Hall steps ordered the men to go away " in the Queen's na MP." But before separat- ing, he wished to inform Mr. Price, in the presence of the people, that he was not wanted in these parts. He , had better be careful of what he did, as the police had had enough of his agitations before. He was not a genuine Warrington working-man. Mr. Price indig- nantly rejoined that he hail been a working-man all his life. The people were then ordered to disperse, and they Proceeded again to the Drill Hall. Finding the door locked, they stayed for a few minutes outside, while Mr. Price denounced Inspector Spinks after which they separated, Mr Price apparently taking credit for having 1 the soup kitchen opened.

At Lvmm Petty Sessions, on Friday, before Mr. T. P. Ncrris, Dr. Brahazon, and Mr. A. Watkin, John Laber- Tier, and Annie Laberner, Newfield, Lymm, were nharged with neglecting their 6 'hildren on the 7th Pebruary, in a manner likPly to iej.n-e tiler health. Mr. Lewin, solicitor, appeared to pros”eute on behalf of the N.S P.C.C. and said that the neglect on the part of the iefendants had been continuous. The parents were alleged to he of drunken habit. Tite male defendant was away most of the time at work and the children were left for four or five we it; at time.—lnspecter McAteer, N S.P.C.C. stated has he visited the defendants hotne on Feb. 2nd

.o company with S^rgeant Gsrner and found the chil iren there but no parents. These children Annie 14- 1mi.12, and Thomas?, and Ruth 4, were all in a very ilthy condition and ill clothed. Their bodies wrre swarming with vermin and lice. Two of them were in' a delicatliand emaciated condition. The male defend- ant. is a fl4tman trading twtween Runcorn, Wigan, and Lvmm, which accounted for his continued absence. On the 7th of this month he again visited the house and there was no imnrevement whatever.—SArgeant Garner corroborated.—The girl Annie was sent for, and she said that whilst her parents were away she was left to take care of the children. She had had several postal orders of from 4s. to ss. and onre 2s. She admitted that the house was not as it ought to have been.—The Bench dismi.sed defendants with a caution. ..„ _ _

Alfred Leather and Jane Leather, Newfi.lds, Lvmm were charged with neelectint, on tip, 2tid February their children, MM', 11 ; Robert. 9; Clara, 3 ; and Daniel.'lo mnnths.—Mr. Lewin prnseeutei in this case, and In- spector McAter stated that h. had visited the def,n- dant's honse with Sergeant Garner on the 2nd Feh.,and found there the two defendant.; and to children. Richard and Daniel. The condition of those children was similar to thnse in the first case. The girl Mars-, was also insufficiently clad, hut of Clara' he know noth- ing.—Sergeant Garner corroborated the °lnspector and detailed the condition of the children.— The bench ultimately derided that the male defendant was the greater culprit and sent him to gaol for one month's bard lahour and the woman was diamiased with a cautim.

The same charge WRS preferred against Joseph and lElizabeth Brazendale, NewPl: Lynam, For negleCting. their children, Jane, George, Nelly., and Joseph on the 2nd February.—lnspector McAteer. had visited the house on the same date as the others and the evidence produced by him was of a similar discript'on, excgat that the children were in a slightly cleaner condition.' Re had visited the house sosin on the 7th, hut there was no improvement. Sergeant Garner said both parents were addicted to drink and he had cautioned them for neglet. It was only a short time since Jane was seen ' begging at a house in Lymm. In this case the bench sent both defendants to gaol for 14 days.

div.head: DETERMINED SUICIDE AT WAR-
div.p: DETERMINED SUICIDE AT WAR-
RINGTON BRIDGE.

A MAN JUMPS INTO TIIE RIVER. A suicide ot a moat determined character was 'committed Friday afternoon between half-Dast one, and two at Warrington bridge. A man was seen to climb the wall of the bridge, and deliberately throw himself into ths river. The water is clear of ice at the spot where he jumped in, hut a little lower down there is a sJlid mass of ice. A window shutter was thrown to the man to help him to keep 'above the water, but he refused to avail himself of its assistance. A man named ,JoQeph Cross, wood turner, Rose and Crown-et., then.pluckily offered to make an attempt to rescue the would be suicide, and he was accordingly lowered down into the water. Before he could reach the drown- ing man, however, the latter Was swept under the ice by the current of the river, and disappeared from view. Cross was then pulled out of the river. It was impossible to grapple for thb man owing to the sheet of ice which covered the river, and up to a late hour last night, the body was not recovered. It was subsequently discovered that the man's name was Dominic or Michael Hogan, a married man, aged 27 years, and residing at School Brow. He leaves one child. He worked at Nelson's Tan- ' nery, and was working. yesterday morning. He then showed no strange symptoms, but it is sur- mised that domestic trouble has caused him to com- mit the rash act.

Council Idgch has —almost, reached the term

for which it was elected has, probably been, the most advanced and progressivemunicipal authority in England.. In every direction in which a local, authority en exert its energies it has set a noble. • example anal accomplished a great work. WHAT is to be said about the Colchester. Colchester election? It certainly cannot by any stretch of iMagination be regarded as the latest evidence of that flowing tide which, it is said, will carry the tfnionists into power at the next election. The return of Sir W. D. PEARSON is a Liberal victory in every sense of the word. Until Tuesday,Colches- ter had for fourteen or fifteen years persistently and consistently returned Tories to the House of Commons. This was not because the Liberals had 4°t contested the seat. Colchester has been a teuch-feught constituency. There was a contested election in 1885, another in 1886, a third—a bye- election—in 1888, and a fourth in 1892. On each asion the Tory came out at the top of the poll, t,leri W. D. PEAnsox, the now successful Liberal, t2g the defeated candidate in 1892. In that leer therefore the election of Tuesday shows a „er gain to the Liberal party. Nor is the Tory d twat to be accounted for by local apathy °II the part of the previously successful Parts. The poll was the highest there has uee° in all the elections ref erred to, and the Tory candidate, although defeated, has actually polled a greater number. of votes than did of his successful predecessors. Desperate were made by the Unionists to bring up !N'er3, available voter, and it is stated that in one .L.,4llBttinee a party of soldiers who we e entitled .1;a Vote but who had been removed to other :Tacks previous to the election were driven a dis- b'nea of thirty-four miles in brakes lent by the crtE of NORFOLK and LORD LONDONDERRY. ei :clarlY, therefore, in view of those circumstances 1,, only lesson that can be deduced from the elec- ,.°° ie that thero has been a decided growth of 4iberalism, at all events in that part of Essex in Which Colchester is situated. We do not see how L1443' other interpretation can be put upon the rajovity of 263 which sends Sir W. D. PEARSON Parliament. As a last resort some Tory news- , rers seem disposed to round upon their midi- . e end blame him for the reverse, but this, after 1111' 18 the meanest and lamest of all ways of ac- for such a decided rebuff. It is an excep- tiori • a'Y poor pretence in the present case, for 1 CaPt • VERERER can still say that he has polled votes in Colchester than any other Tory .7udidate. He will probably be disposed also to that the "flowing tide" is a myth.

BILLIARDS. A billiard match between the members of. the Runcorn Volunteer Social Club and the members of the Widnes Conservative Club took place in the Drill Hall, Runcorn, on Saturday. Thirteen games were played, Runcorn securing 1,950 points and Widnes 1,681, or a majority for Runcorn of 269. The visitors generally commented upon the improve- ment in the room by its extension, and favourably remarked upon the excellent tables which had been purchased. PARISH CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOLS, RUNCORN. The teachers and friends attending the Parish Church Sunday Schools held a social gathering on Friday evening. The guests present included the Revs. A. J. Jameson and 11. G. Firth. The Vicar the Rev. Canon Wood) was unable to be present. The party partook of a well-served supper, and dur- ing the evening engaged in a number of recreative games. The proceedings were agreeably inters- persed with singing. ST. JOHN AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION, RUNCORN. On Wednesday afternoon, the examination of the members of this Association was held. Dr. L. Morgan, of Liverpool, was the examiner and he expressed himself .well pleased with the way the members of the class acquitted themselves. Thirty persons presented themselves for examination. Dr. McDougall (lecturer), Mr. S. Henderson (hon. trea- serer),Mr. Banks (chairman of committee), and Mr, H.Clare (hon.secretary),were present. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded Dr. Morgan for the manner he had conducted the examination. Sr. PAUL'S BIBLE CLASS, RUNCORN. What is termed an "open meeting" in connection with this class was held on Sunday afternoon. There was a large attendance. The meeting was presided over by Mr. B. Kmveton. Two selections on piano and organ were given by Mr. William Cooke and Mr. G. Rowley, who also accompanied on these instruments during the afternoon. A recita- tion was exceedingly well given by Mr. Littler, entitled " The Amen Corner." The soloists were Mrs. Temperley " Eternity " ; Mrs. A. Caygill "Come ever smiling liberty"; Miss Heatherington "Calvary"; and Mr. Morris "If rith all your hearts.' SEAMEN'S INSTITUTE, RUNCORN. In this Institute, on Tuesday evening, the usual weekly entertainment was provided, when there was a large attendance. Mr. Oxworth presided. Songs were given by Miss Douglas, Miss G. Water- worth, and Messrs. W. Rovrbottom, A. Robley, A. Harrison, H. Taylor, J. H. Platts,William Cresswell, and M. Brown. A mouth organ solo was well ren- dered by Mr. G. Finney, and recitations were con- tributed by Miss A. Evans, Miss G. Waterworth,Mr. Hulse, and Mr. H. Roper. Readinga were given by Mr. A. Waterworth. The various items were well given, and an enjoyable evening was spent. PRINIITIIE METHODIST CHRISTIAN ENDEAVOLTE SOCIETY. A Band of Hope entettainment promoted by this society was held in the Primitive Methodist school- room, Greenway-road, on Wednesday evening. There was a large attendance. An address on tem- perance was delivered by Mr. Page. A solo was sung by Miss Wright, and recitations were given by the following :—Mr. G. Aston and the Misses Beatrice Stubbs, Ada Fleet, Miles, M. Shingler, L. Poole, A. tlarrop, C Williams, and K. Williams. A vote of thanks WaS passed to Sir. Aston for his ser- vices in arranging the entertainment, on the pro- position of Mr.W. Gittins, seconded by Mr. Richar- dson. RUNCORN FCHOOL BOARD EVENING CONTINUATION

div.p: VICTIMS.

On Sunday afternoon the funeral took place of the two young men named Frederick Leathwoed,of Halton View, Widnes, and James Howard, of Simm's Cross, Widnes, who were drowned whilst skating on the river Dee, a little above the village of Farndon, on Tuesday. The remains of Frederick Leath wood were interred in Farnworth churchyard. The friends met at the residence of the parents of deceased, Halton View. The fuueral cortege con- tained a procession consisting of about 100 mem- bers of the Hearts of Oak Lodge; 100 Oddiellows, and a large number of the workers at the Silver and Copper Works, and also several coaches con- taining relatives and friends. Among those who sent conveyances, and who followed in the proces- sion, were Mr. Clarke, who was accompanied by Councillor Barlow (one of the managers of the Alkali Works) ; Mr. F. Barlow, and Mr. Foreham ; Councillors Wright and Christie ; Alderman Ware- ing, Councillors Bullough, Oittens and ()there. All along the route the blinds of the houses were drawn, and sympathy was everywhere manifested. Arrived at Farnworth, the body was met by the Vicar of St. Ambrose's (the Rev. G. A. Le 113 rt), the Vicar of Farnworth (the Rev. J. Wright. Williams), and the Rev. F. Nightingale. A large number of wreaths had brnjn sent, conspicuous among which was an artificial one subscribed for by the etn ploy6s at the Copper Works, through the instru- mentality of Mr. Dowers, the timekeeper. The ' cortege then returned to Simms' Cros., (Robert- road), where the body of the young man James Howard lay. Six coaches containing the relatives, as well as a large number of conveyances followed the hearse to Sankey churchyard, the place of in- terment The Widnes; Volunteers, under the com- mand of Captain Lewis, jOitlod in the procession. The country roads were thranged with people,most of whom had come from Widnes. The coffin was taken into Sankey church,where part of the service was read by the Rev*. Le Bert and Nightingale, the remaining portion being pronounced at the grave- eide. RuNConN STIOOTING CLUB. Ashton the chair was occupied by Captain 0. Ashton, and the vice-chair by Lieutenant Brnintrit. A number of toasts were honoured. Sergeants Player and Callighan re- sponded to the toast of "The Past and Present Drill Instructors." Sergeant Woodland submitted his report and balance sheet for the year 1891, in which he stated that during the past year the in- tere,stm of the club had been fully maintained. The shooting of the younger members had im- proved, end they attended with wonderful regu- latity. The new gold medal ler the purchase of .which the club was mainly indebted to Capt. On wednesdat, evening, the first smoking concert in connection- with the club took place and was attended by a good number of local wheelers. It was held under the presidency of Dr. McKenzie, in the fine billiard room of the George and Dragon Hotel. Songs were contributed by Mr. Norman (St. Helens). Mr. Clare, Mr. A. Shingler, Mr. J. Witherington, Mr. Mack and Mr. Whinyates. The singing of Mr. Norman was highly appreciated, and ' he was several times encored. Several toasts were proposed and duly honoured. The Chairman in the course of a short address thought the large gathering augured well for the season 1E95. As a medical man, he thought there was no pastime more invigorating and better for the physical development of the body than' cycling. He hoped the Runcorn Cycling Club would be as successful as the football club had been. She illustrated her subject by a number of drawings and exhibi- tions of several insects' nests. INDEPENDENT LABOUR PARTI—RUNCORN BRANCH. .

On Sunday afterricTo—n—a—p-üblic meeting of the I.L.P . was held in Forrester's Hall, when about 300 persons assembled to hear a lecture on Socialism by Mr. Gregory, of Manchester. The chairman was Ur. Boyle, of Widnes. Several additional members were enrolled. BIRTHDAY CELEBRATION AT RUNCORN. . .

A. substantial supper in celebration of the birth- day of Mr. Henry Darlington,was served at the Rail- way Hotel,on Friday evening. A number of toasts was proposed and duly honoured. Dlr. W. M. Wil- liams presented Mr. Darlington with a handsome pair of slippers, subscribed for by several friends. Sings were given during the evening by Messrs. W M. Williams, Crawford, Hill, E. Newton, and Leach.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT INQUIRY AT WIDNES.

At the Town Hall, Widnea, on Thursday morning, a local government inquiry was held by Mr. Hienze Walton C.E., with regard to the application of the Widnes Cor- poration for sanction to borrow certain sums for works of public and private street improvement, for the pup. chase of land for a cemetery ' • and for sewerage works. There were present Alderman Sadler, Lilly,and Willis son, Councillors T. Smith, W. Christie, H. fl. Shores, T. Shuttleworth, W. liodgkinson, S. Quinn, Messrs. H. S. Oppenheim (town clerk), T. Craik (deputy town clerk), S. Hoyle (accountant), J, S: Sinclair (Surveyor) and Dr. MacLennan (medical officer). The Town Clerk ‘xplained the various items of their application, viz : £1,720 for the improvement in Peel House-lane; £1.098 15.. Bd. for the improvement of main roads, in Albert-road, Victoria-rsad, and Halton View ; £691 for part of Albertroad and part of Halton View; £lO,OOO for street improvements, mainly for hack pass- ages in the neighbourhood of West Dank. 'Fins applica- tion was nude in order to enable the property owners to pay back the amount expended by instalments. £lOO for Sewerage, extending from Castle-street to Warring- toe-road. There was no opposition to these improve- ments. With regard to the provision ot a cemetery the Towu Clerk traced the history of the movement, and I showed that the matter was under the consideration of the old Local Board, and that after the incorporation of the borough, the Town Council took up the subject. By inquiries they found that it was necessary to have a place of sepulcher belonging ta the town, insomuch as that the accommodation at S'...Luke's,St.ldary's, and St. Dede's was becoming limited. Lie gave statistics show- ing the number of burials, the grave space, and the population in each of the parishes named. He then pointed out how ttrat the Corporation having decided that a cemetery was necessary, advertised for sites with the result that among the offers was ems for a portion of the Moss Brook estate.. hater on negotiations were entered into for the purchase of the whole estate at more advantageous term.. The site contained 49 acres and the price asked was £5',000. A further sum of £2OO was re- quired to defray cert tin expenses connected with the purchase of the minerals from the Duchy of Lancaster. The distance of the proposed cemetery was little more than a mile from the Town flall.—The Surveyor con- firmed the statement of the Town Clerk, and expressed the opinion that the extanaion•of ttie present graveyards was not feasible on manittry grounds.. This view was confirmed by Dr. MacLennan, and Councillor Hodgkin- son. Councillor Christie opposed the scheme, and said that however &simple it might be to have a cemetery, he considered that the burial accommodation at St. Luke's, with the additions that could be made, would be sufficient for 59 years to come. As is new borough they I.tad lots el work to do, which were matters of urzency. He also minted out that the Town Council , had decided in favour of a cemetery by the casting vote of the Mayor. it was subsequently stated. however,that the proposed site had been unanimously passed, wh •rn- upon .Ir. Christie said that he voted against it, having persistently opposed the scheme from the beginning. The Mayor proposed a vote of thanks to the Inspec- t nta, Mr. Christie seconded. The Inspector responded and said the prowedings bad been very harmonious and wished :ill enquiries to be the same.

D'OTLY CARTES COMIC OPERA COMPANY* The patrons of Mr. Wallace Revill's hand,, 'me new Theatre Royal and Opera House St. Helens, will be - afforded an exceptional musical treat next week. As ' will be seen from an advertisement in another eislumei arrange nents have been completed for & visit by Mr. D'Oyly Carte's famous Comic Opera Company in their two great successes "Toe Chieftain" and the well-knowia " H.M.S. Pinafore." The company is an admirable or. in every respect and includes some of the best known artistes in that particular branch of theatrical representation. The words of " The Chieftain" are by Mr. F. C. Hartland the well. known editor of " Punch " for many rare, and the music has been composed by Sir Arthur Sullivan. Its recent production in the Metropolis was a brilliant suc- cess, and there can be no doubt that Mr. Revill's enter. prise deserves. the unstinted support of the people of St. Helens and district. It is to be hoped that large houses will greet the performances, and that the stay of the Opera Company in the town may be one run of •SUCCESSe. " The Chieftain " will be presented on Mondar.Tuesday. Friday aud Saturday, and H.M.S. Pinafore" on Wed- nesday and Thursclay. The performance each evening will be preceded by an amusing oporetta entitled, . " Quite an adventure."

Sir E. GREY informed Mr. LABOCCRERE that In cone quence of authoritative information received by her Majesty's Government at one time during the recess, steps were taken to acertain if, in the opinion of the other Governments of Europe and the Government of the United States, there was any possibility of bringing about a peace between China and Japan on certain terms. The replies were generally favourable, but they could not be published at present. Sir H. Jamas asked leave to move the adjournment of , the House in order to call attention to the recent inaposi- tion of duties on the impartation of cottsn manufac- tures and 3 arns into India from England. Sir Elgarer • being suppoited by nearly all the Opposition members.' the majority of the Unionists, and a few Liberals, leave was given. The right hon, gentleman said the textile industry in India had become a serious competitor with ! this country in some twigs markets, but all that Lau- • cashire asked was that the race should be run at level - rates, And that a dead weight should not be imposed on Lane shire. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD INSPECTOR'S VISIT. Mr. Dansey (Local Government Board inspector) said he wanted to cell the attention of the Board to one or two matters relating to the WA-khouse. He was not at i all satisfied with the present nursing arrangements. There was no paid nurse on night duty, the patients in the hospital being in eharge of irresponsible paupers dot- ing the night. There were one or two patients who needed constant attention, and if there were two nurses they could divide the night duty. There was also the question of further accommodation for the men. The young men's room had, for several years, been full, so that two men had to sleep in the fever ward and the caretaker in the infectious diseases ward. It was neces- sary that further accommodation should be provided.. ,He also complained that the children's boots were too heavy, too stiff and too narrow, to allow the feet te expand.—The Chairrasn said that the matters referred to by the Inspector would receive attention. The Cheshire County Council elections are now near at hand, but it is not at all likely that there wilP be Is contest in Runcorn. This, or course, will Minitely known to-day (Friday), which is the last day for nominations to be handed in. With Major Harlehurst's resignation there is a vacancy in the North Division. Only one candidate is at present known to have entered the field, and this is Mr. S. Taylor, if., who has filled many important positions in the town. Ile has hem promised the support of many Influential electnr6 and will, no doubt,if:elected,fill the position with'codit t him- self and the town. THE AGED PEOPLE'S TREAT AT RUNCORN.

In the Public flail the aged people of Runcorn were on Tuesday evening provided with their annual treat Elaborate preparations had been made to make the treat A success, and for several weeks a num her of com- mittees have been at work. The names of the gentle- men comprising these committees have already ap- peared in the " Examiner," so that it is unnecessary to recapitulate them, but it should be stated that the ar- rangements were admirably carried our,reflecting great credit on all concerned. During the afternoon a band of ladies were busily engaged cutting up the required viands, with printed instructions to " Please cut the bread and hotter thin." At five o'clock tea was served, at which 399 persons were present. whose ages ranged from 60 years to 86. There were 281 females and 118 males, some of the oldest persons present were :—. • ry Robinson, Shaw-sr. ; Anna Woodier, Peel-st. ,• Eljz&th Winterbotham, Bridgeltt::Ann Toilet% Nelson. t ; Betsy Hewitt. div.head: QUESTION OF DISINFECTION.
div.p: THE QUESTION OF DISINFECTION.

Mr. Williams referring to the subject of disinfection of clothing and bedding from dwellings wherein scarlet fever or other infectious disease might occur, which was introduced at the last meeting, said the necessity far this course had been accentuated by the repeated outbreaks of sitarlet fever in more than one part of the Union, and it was the opinion of Dr. Adams • that as long as no effectual meana were adopted for destroying the germs, they would he subject to fresh attacks from time to time, although there might have been intervals of some dura- tion during which no development had taken place. Clothing, blankets, rugs, and other coverings used about a patient, or in the same room, and probably wn- used for months, might on being opened out or used, disseminate the latent germs, and again produce a crop of cases. There did not appear to be any known cer- tainty of destroying those seeds of disease in the case of bedding, carpets, and heavy woollens, especially, except I the exposure to great heat, and if the Council were to take effectual steps to prevent the spread of infec- tion in the Vahan, they must not grudge such cost as might be incuried in an doing. That, how- ever, need not be more than a fractional addition to their sanitary expenditure. The Council had already a disinfector, and a van for removing clothing, and bedding from infected houses. They would require occasional horse bower for fetching and returning articles, a man to attend the same an additional ton of coal two or three times a year, and some remuneration to be given to the caretaker's husband—Eccleshall. The Council would also have to lend bedding in some cases for use, whilst infected goods were being stored. In order to discuss the different matters of detail, and to bring some plan forward for the consideration of the Council, he moved that the following councillors form a committee for such purpose, and to cansult with Dr. Adams, the result to ;le reported at the next meeting of the Council :—The Chairman, Messrs. Heywood, Stokes, WoWilliams, odward, Brandreth, Williams Chadwick, Davenport, and Itaxtef.—Mr. Stokes seconded, and the motion was carried.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A DECEITFUL PAtwrza.

On Monday morning., at the Borough Police Court, before the Mayor (chairman), and other magistrates. Henry Skelding, painter, 8 Hill-street, was charged with stealing by means of a trick. from Rohert Smart, con- fectioner, on the llth inst., the sum of 54. in.cash —Mr. Hunt (chief constable) said that complainant occupied premises at 28. Q leen-street, and on the day named pri- soner had some talk with Mr. Smart about painting a van belonging to the latter. Arrangements were . made and prisoner. prevailed upon Mr. Smart to give him ss. to procure paint, saving that he could get it cheaper than complainant. Not torn* up for a few days the matter was reported to the police who apprehended prisoner.— Mr. Smart, complainant, after corroborating Mr. Hunt, said the prisoner had done some work for him about three months before. The van had been,scraped by a youth since the arrangement with prisoner, and pre- sumably by his direction, hut he himself had never turned on. He was to have been paid 355. for the job. —Mr. Hunt stated that while prisoner had been doing nothing his wife had been going dilly for soup.—ln court prisoner said he had receivd the money on ac- count, and when asked what he had done with it said, "I've laid it out, but not in paint,.l'm sorry to say."— Mr. Monk.. one of the magistrates, thought it an unwise thing for Mr. Smart to lend the defendant the money so readily.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for 14 days' hard. labour.

EXEMPLARY PUNISHMENT FOR A SHOP DOOR THIEF-, At the Borough Police Court, on Monday morning, before the Mayor (Councillor James Fsirclougli) and other magistrates, William Richardson, labourer, no ad-. dress, was charged with stealing from the shop-door of Messrs. linsworth Bros., D., Ly,m-.-gt' . on Saturday afternoon, 9 scarves, a alue s.3.—The Chief Camstahie stated that the defendant was a tramp, arid about 4, o'clock on Saturday afternoon the bundle of wool scarves in question was hanging up just inside the shop-door. At 5 o'clock they were gone, The mat- ter was reported to the police. and Dstective Monag- han end Sergeant Cheney made inquiries. Monaghan found the prisoner in the " Golden Grove" puhlic- house with some of the scarves in his possession. The others, he said., he had sold for 21. e ,ch.—Prisoner was soot to gaol for:two months' hard labour. " SHORT OF A SHILLING BUT WORTH £3 000 At the Boroush Police Court, on Wednesday- morning, before Mr. J. Geddes, Richard Thomas Martindale was chargoci with attoms ting to obtain 1. by false sisetences from John Henry G Mena, on Tuesday, the 19-h inst.— Mr. Gittens, the complainant. stated that at 830 on Tuesday evening the prisoner came to his efli,-e in Buttermatket-stret and stated that lie had 18 houses which he wanted the complainant to collect the rents for. An anpointnient for 9 30 was made, but before leaving, defendant asked for it. to go back to G arirtie, where he professed to be a native. Notwithstanding this demand defendant statod to complainant that he was "worth £3 000, poor as he looked," Ile also profes:ed to be the owner of ten houses in Knutsford-road, and that he had barn twice to South America. Mr. Gittens was, hnwever, suspicious, and not only refused to lend defendant the is. but also gaite: information to D tective. IVlonagtan.—Menaglian denntedtthat frnm the informs- thin of last witness he Went us search of defendant and found him in a common lodging-house at Town's End, The officer brought him down to the police station and charged him, but received no reply. Witness had reasons to believe that defendant had obtained money from painters in the town on the preßece nt rejuvenating his fictitious houses.—A remand of 24 hours was granted in order that inquiries he made. On Thursday before Mr. S. Cbandley; Alderman Sutton and the Mayor, the prisoner was brought up and charged with obtaining, by means of a trick, is. from: Mr. J. Bedgecock, on Monday and also charged with obtaining lodgings from Ann Davies to the extent of is. After hearing, the evidence produced the previous day,, Mr. Efedgecock said the prisoner came to him on Monday night about 6 o'clock, and after a short conversation said he owned. six houses on Liverpool-road and wanted an estimate for tho painting of them I.3sfore ' leaving, prisoner prevailed upon witness to lend him a shilling to retorts to Gelborne. Defendant had stated that he lived in E Icsmere-street, E,srlestawn.—An n Davies, hedging-house keeper, Hill-street,said the prisoner cause en Saturday night and told her that he worked on the London and North-Western Railway. He asked if she had room for three mare lodgers he would brims,,and who would pay weekly. On Sunday morning he followed her out and persuaded her to give him , stating that he had six houses in Runcorn.. Prisoner stay ed three nights at a cost of 4d. each night and she had received nothing for it. He also made a promise to find her hus- band work,—The Magistrate's Clerk stated that among his other delintmences prisoner had ordered a tombstone at Stockton Heath.—The bench ordered prisoner to gaol for 14 days en each charge (6 we ks in all). ANOTHER MARKET' PICKPOCKET. . _ - .

On Thursday morning, at the Borough Police Court, ! before Mr. S. Chant?ley and the Mayor, Sarah Digman,' York-st., Leeds, pleaded guilty to the charge of stealing from the person of Louisa Elizabeth Hughes in the War- rington Mal ket-place on Wednesday, a purse contai n rig 129. 8,1. in cish and nine Co-operative checks.—The Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) said the complainant was the wife of Joseph Hughes, 86 Longford-st., Warrington, and that defendant was 63 sears 4:r age and a native of Dublin, but the address gitien above was supposed tube hers. She came to Warrington on Wednesday morning ! and since her capture had refused to give any particu- lars to the police. On the day in question the corn- plainant was in the lower market shed. The prisoner was also there, and several women thinking her actions suspicious watched her and eventually saw her push against Mrs. Hughes, lift up her jacket and take out the purse. According to Mr. Hunt the women watching "went for her like very wolves," and a crowd rapidly collected. It was in a sense fortunate' that Detective , Sergeant Monaghan was near to, to receive the prisoner in charge and protect her from the said " wolves." She drorni ii the purse aud was taken to the, police station . where on being searched 9a. 51. was found upon her, ' also a small hand-basket. The wowian was known to many people by sight, and Mr. Place, the market in- spector, had seen her about the buildings. There had been a great deal of pocket-pUting of late and Mr. Hunt asked for one week's remand in rrdtir that inquiries might be made and as he thought the prisoner was "old" in inure ways than one.—The Bench granted a remand of seven days.

Mr. Foster : lam not doing wit Mr. Fairclough but with him (pointinei to defendant).
