ALLEUED WILFUL DAXIAGE TO PROPERTY.

Before Mr. S. Chandley and the Mayor at Warrington Borough Police Court, on Thursday, Ellen McEvoy, 9, Shop-yard, was charged with having wilfully and mali- ciously damaged a c.rtain cottage, ownad by Messrs.S. and William Wilcock Rowe.

Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the defendant,and Mr. J. Shaw Green prosecuted on bchalf of the owners, and said he had the care of some property in Bank-st., part of it being uninhabited,and the cottage in question was classed amongst tilose. For some time past he had had comolaints about the damage which was done there,and on Tuesday,the 12th inst., a message came to his office, in consequence of which he sent one of his clerks down to the property, and he found that considerable damage had been done within an hour or so. While there he overheard SOITIP conversation between three women,one of whom was defendant. This was the reason he had taken out the tr. m mons. _

air. Charles [-Daley, the clerk who went down to see the property, said that while standing in the shadow of one of the houses in the yar /, he heard the defrnds,nt say she had got a lot of timber in her pantry. On this witness stepped out and asked her about it,'a,nd defend- ant add she hal got it from the cottages. Witness then int4rmed a polibe officer. Mr. Davies : How long is it since the cottage was tenanted?

Witness : Eight years. Mr. Dailies : How long has it been a danger to the public? . Witness: Not until the damage was done In answer to Mr. Davies he also stated that the flaor which had disappeared had been probably taken by the defendant and that the gable end of the cottage had certainly not been blown away by the gale as Mr. Davies bad stated. There had not been any door to the cottage since the 12th. Mr. Davies : Ras any attempt been made to repair the building during the last nine years. Witness : No. In answer to further questions he swore that the gable end of the house was pulled down wiltully and not by decay, P.C. Barlow stated that on the 13th of the present month, from instructions he had received, he and P.C. Hardie went down into Ship Yard and visited the deten- dant's house aini Fi-ked where the timber was, and,de- Pendant said it was in the pantry. Witness proceeded therp and found the place blocked .tvvith large pieces and about 1 cwt. of small pieces, ,Defendant told him she had tak m it out of " those old;bnildings." :Witness then reported the case to Mr. Shaw-Green. Mr. Davies, tor the defence, declared that the case was ridiculous. div.head: CONCEALMENT OF BIRTH AT HA:I"FON. POLICE PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: THE CONCEALMENT OF BIRTH AT HA:I"FON. POLICE PROCEEDINGS.

At the Warrington Oecasional Court on Thursday, before Mr. H. N'eld, Ada Maddock, Hatton, was charzed that on F ,bruary 3rd, being delivered of a female child, she unlawfully endeavoured ta conceal the birth thereof. Superintendent Atherton, of Runcorn, watched the pro- ceedings on behalf of the police. Mary Maddock said, that she was a single woman residine at flattan The defendant was her daughter and had been in service, until about two months ago. She then came home, and witness noticed tier condition. Upon being questioned, the defendant. denied being in the condition suspected. Although asked several times she always denie3 it until near the last, when she gave no answer at all. On Thursday, February 741, witness noticed her daughter looking ill, and upon beim," again questioned, she admitted giving birth to a child, which eh said was in a room upstairs. They then went un- Stairs, and found the child coverbd up upon a table near theavindow. The child was dead. She examined the child, and found no marks extent one at the back of the head. Witness went for Dr. Bowers next day, and he came the same evening to ere her daughter. Hr dauviter had never told her that she expected to be confined, nor any preparations Made. S'lo had had child previously—eighteen months ago. The room where the child's body was found had not been used for sleeping for about four years. On Sunday, February 3rl, witness was away from home all the afternoon. Dr. Bawers, Strettnn, saidthat on February Stb, t e last witness came to his hnnae and asked him to come to see her ilaug,hter. 'Be went to the house about six o'clock. On going upstairs into the baekroorn he found the body of a full-grown newly barn female child. M. told the mother and daughter that information would have to be given to the police. He asked the prisoner why she did not make more preparation, and get assist- ance, and she replied that she did not wish anyone to know. Witness afterwards gave information to P.O Pratt, the same evening. He afterwards made a post- mortem examination by order of the coroner, and came to the coaclusion that the child had never Aired. The only mark on the body was one at the back of the head which in his opinion was caused during birth. P.C. Brett, stationed at Stretton, said that he appre- hended the prisoner that morning at her mother's house. He Charged her with concealment ef birth, but she made no reply. After he had been informed of the circum- stances by Dr.Bewers.be had asked prisoner why she had not reported it sooner, and she replied that her mother had always been on to her about it since she came Flame and she was afraid. Mr. Nield, in giving his decision, said, that prisoner bad had a very near "shave." It was a very serious matter indeed. Fie thought the mother of the prisoner was also ver%. much to blame, as her daughter was lodging in die same room, and she was an experienced woman. A great deal of blame, therefore, lay upon her. He hoped that she would take a lesson from it, as it might have been a more serious charge. The case would be dismissed.

div.p: UR. GLADSTONE AND THE SABBATH

In Mr.Glaclstone's article on " The Lord's Day," which is to appear in the March number of the " Church Monthly," the ex-Premier insists very strongly that a periodical day of rest " is a necessity of health as well tor the brain of man as for the general fabric of his body," although he is not aware that this opinion has ever been made the subject of sanitary statistics. In regard to the Divine obligation of the observance of the Sabbath,Mr.Gladstone is at pains to show that the charge from the seventh day to the first was authoritativey made. "The seventh day of the week," he sass, " has been deposed from its title to obligatory religious oh- servance, and its prerogative has been carried over to the first, under no direct precept of Scripture, but yet with a Biblical record of facts, all supplied by St. John, which go far towards showing that among the Apostles themselves, and therefore from Apostolic times,the prac- tice of Divine worship on the Lord's Day has been con- tinuously and firmly est tblished." Indeed, so strongly does Mr. Gladstone defend his thesis, that in summing up his arguments on this head he says :—" No Chris- tian can entertain a reasonable doubt as to the solidity of the foundations on which the established tradition and practice rest." The article is bound to excite wide- spread interest. Mr. Gladstone intimates that in a further paper he will deal with that portion of he sub- ject OM which the prevailing conceptions are "the most lame and incomplete"'

div.head: BILL NYE, THE FAMOUS AMERICAN
div.p: BILL NYE, THE FAMOUS AMERICAN
HUMORIST.

Nestled away in the mountains of North Carolina lives " Bill Nye," the hoinoriA. It is said of this particular region of North Carolina that within any ter. square miles of the country everything necessary to the comfort and happiness of man can be produced. And it is quite certain that within much less than ten miles a certain famous man firr s all that sustains him for his arduous task of continuing to make people laugh—a devoted wile, four lovely children, and a home which is ideal in every reswct. Probably there are few if any,Arnerican ati hors who make more by their writings than does " Bill " Nye, whose real name is, by the way, Edgar Wilson Nye. Certainly there is no more indefatigable worker. He contributes to newspapers all over the United States, and so far his popularity has never waned for a moment. Mr. Nye's house was the work of a celebrated architeat, and is an ideal home. The farm consists of seventy-five acres, and includes all the fruits for which the country is celebrated. Between the house and the river there is a peach orchard of twenty acres, and on each side are vineyards and other fruits. The house it- self is a Ilia, broad one. According to Mr. Nye it is a sort of Cc.lonial Queen Anne, " with a Watteau back."

The part,culars were gathered by Mr. Mohun, the UNited States agent in the Congo Free State, trom two of the natives who took part in the murder IntrA and I (said Mr. Motion's informant) were standing next to tile Pasrir, and at a sign from the chief we seized him by the artni as he was sitting in kis chai.a. He turned and asked what -re meant. Kinena looked at him arid said, " Pasha, Woo have got to die Bruin turned, and exclaitned rather angrily," What do yau mean ? Is this a joke . Who are you, that you can give orders for a man to die ?" Kinena replied, " I di not give the orders,l receive them trom Kibong,, who is my chief ; arid when Kibonge gives an order to ma I ittey it." E 11111 read the letter and saw that it was true. Drawing a I breath, he turned and said you may kill me, hut atm% think I am the only white man in the country. There are many others who will he willing to avenge lIIV drth; and let run tell you that in less then two years from now there won't be an Arab left in the entire country now held by your people." No fear was hown by Emin, but when he spoke of having care taken if his little daughter lie trembled slightly. We held to him for a few moments ; then arose, and left the body where it was." Afterwards Mamba severed the head from the bedy, and Kinena had it wicked in a small box and sent on to Kibouge, to E how that his orders ha d been obeyed.
LIBERAL VICTORY AT COLCHESTER.

--- The polling at Colchester on Tuosday resulted in a clecis' ve Liberal victory, Sir W. Pearson gaining the seat by the handsome majority of 263 votes. The figures were—Pearson, 2,559 ; Vereker, 2 296. At the last elec- tion the Tories won by 61 votes. The poll was very heavy.

pEeifeETH. SERIOUS COLLISION —On Sunday night about 7.30 as a landau belong-' e to Messrs. Dixon and Fletcher,Gros- venor Hotel. IT idnes, was on its way to Widnes, a horse attached so a heavy trap, came dashing along at a mad gallop ,and smashed into the landau. There was so ~ever with the trap. There were several Widnes gen- ' tlemen in the landau, who, however.escaped any injury. The horse in the tr la was thrown violently to the ground and was raised with difficulty. It, however, sustained no serious hurt. The landau was smashed badly about the springs and its occupants found it necessary to leave it in the village and walk home to Widnes. The owner of the trap, John Hnrabin Ditton, came up in hot haste soon after the eellision, and gave an account of the horse's sudden bolt. He and some other gentlemen were riding in the trap, when their weight broke one of the shafts. He repaired the damage temporarily, and was leading the horse home, when as they came to Bold Rock Hole, the horse suddenly sprang forward and tore off. He pursued as fast as possible but was too late to prevent tee accident. It is remarkable that mere dam- age was not done, as, had it been any other but Sunday night, the horse would certainly have met other con- veyances in its rush of two or three miles. --- BURIAL 010 UNBAPT tSED INFANTS. feel ‘:unstrained to call attention to what I can Only desc7fDe as a pitiable circumstmc.i in these ad- vanced days of Christian light awl culture. Itnently, as have learned from an entry in the registry or burials in the Cemetery,an infant,whe did not live long enough to receive the rite of Christian baptism, was buried in the Consecrated ground without the rite of Christian burial. The infant is described in the registry merely by the surname of the parents, with the words " unbap. tised " prefixed thereto. Of course I am aware that there are cler9,y in the Anglican Church who weuld refuse the rite of Christian burial to any who had not received the rite of Christian baptism. Whether any such clerly are in this locality Ido not know. Nor do I know whether in this particu- lar instance the parents of the child desired or were re- fused the observance of Christian burial for the little one who breathed but a few houri. But inasmuch as! can easily imaeine that cases of the kind might arise, in which the feelings of the parents would be sadly hurt by the withholding of such rites from the dead unbaptised infant, I write these lines to intimate that any Nonconformist minister would be found wil- ling to render the service which the high sacramental views of an Anglican clergyman would make conscien- tiously impossible for him to discharge. It is not my object to provoke controversy, and I merely wish to intimate that in the event of such cases occurring, I think the registrar of the cemetery should be instructed to tell the parents interested, 'hat there are Christian ministers in the town who would not think it in any sense wrong, but in every sense right for their little ones who died without baptism to be laid in "God's acre" with the reverence and affection that are due to the feeblest lambi of the fold of the Good Shep• herd.—Yours faithfully,
percentage
JOAN YONGE.

Bo much for the Anglo-Saxon ehl wilt conclude by citing the Chief Justice of Eng- aind, A.D. 1260. Chief Justiciary Bracteu, in the reign of Henry 111., in his great work "On the laws and con- stitutions of England," lays down the civil law of the country thus :—" It is to be noted concerning the juris- diction of superior and inferior courts, that in the first place, as the Lord Pope hag ordinary jurisdiction over all in spirituals, so the King bast in toe realm, in temporals. To the Pope and the priesthood belong spiritual things; to the king and the kingdom those that are teropore, as it is said • rho heaven of heavens is the Lord's, but the earth Re has given to the children of men.' Hence, the Pope has nothing,' to do with the dis- pensation of temporal affairs, and more than kings and princes have with the spiritual, lest either should put his sickle to the others harvest. And so the Pope can 1 ordain in the 'aporitual sphere concerning orders and dignities, so also an the king in temporals concerning grants of inheritanc.e and assignment of heire." Rovera drawing level with Everton at Ever- atter having been beaten by Liverpool, the week "eKteasly. It was thought that after that mishan,and esti alter Everton's brilliant display against Bolton "fichriderers, the previous week, that the tie was almost a certainty for the " Toffeemen." Notts Forest also showed that the 5-0 beating they got at Liverpool a few weeks ago, was all wrong, by beating their forns-r con- querors, on the same ground by 2-0. to,, ..ter. lest Bromwich Albion did not actually win at Shef- field against the United,but they did the next best thing, by drawing, and thus having another chance. Sunder- land with a very mixed and almost ragged team got the upper hand of Preston North End who have got no further in the ctip hunt this year than last. Wolverhamp- ton Wanderers and Stoke had previously met twice thia season without' a goat having been scored, but tbe Wolves managed to come out all right in the cup tie, although had the match been played at Stoke, the brot would probably have been on the other leg. ----- Bolton Wanderers and Bury are very near ad very keen rivals. The" Trotters" as a rule do jot shine against the " Shakers,".:even on their egn ground, but they rose to the occasion on Saturday, and won by a goal to none. The match was very vet! fought out. The remaining two matches, Sheffiell Wednesday v. Middlesborough, and Aston Villa v. Newcastle United were practically gilts to the first aamed in each case. It is still a matter of uncertainty as to who will get the cup this year, but surely by inis time, it is the turn of Sheffield Wednesday. -Jo every oc,-asion since 1886 have they reached ti.e last eight in the competition and have several time, got to the semi-final, and once to the final. It is simular that they should have so manv slips between ther.l:up and lip, and surely their turn will come

at last. -- ruere were no first league matches on Saturday, but there were several second league matches. Darwen strengthened their chance of taking part in the test matches, by easily defeating Crewe Alexandra.who must have given up all hope now of getting out of the bot- tom position. The position of the clubs at the top of the second league havechang,ed considerably during the past few weeks. Bury of course are a certainty for the pre- naier position but the second and third are not so cer- tain. It looked at one time, almost certain that Grims- by Town would finish second, but owing to a series of disasters, they are now almost out of the running even for the third place. Notts County, though second at present, are on sufferance there becausa they have played more matches, and Newton Heath and Dar:Yen are in relatively better positions. The last two with Bury will most probably be the aspirants for a position in the first league. The re-played cup ties between Everton and Black- burn Rovers, and West Bromwich Albion and Sheffield United, were brought to a definite conclusion on Wed- rwsday afternoon. West Brornwich Albion also beat Sheffield United by two goals to r.lel and thus justified 1 the general expectation.

As this round decides who shall enter the semi-final, there will be some determined battles between the eight clubs concerned. Sunderland on their own ground should account for Bolton Wanderers uretty easily. The Trotters almost invariably beat Sunderla,rld at Bolton, but it Ls different when they have to go to the banks of the Wear, Aston Villa should also stand a good chance against Notts Forest. The Sheffield Wednesday v. Everton tie is a puzzle, and it is better not to prophecy at all. The Wednesdayites have beaten Everton this Reason at Sheffield, but so have Blackburn Bovera at Blackburn, and yet they failed on Wednesday. The remaining tie between West Bromwich Albion and Wolverhampton Wanderers will rouse great interest in the Black Country, and a monstre gate may be expected. The Albion with the adYantage of ground should win.

BRUNNER, MOND, AND CO., LIMITED.

--- B ALF-YEAHLY MEETING. The 28th half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of Brunner, Mond, and Co., Limited, at Winnington, Northwich, was held on Thursday, in the Law Rooms, Cook-st., Liverpool. Mr. John T. Brunner, M.P. (chair- man of directors), presided, and there was a large attendance. The directors report which we published last week, and which recommended a dividend of 30,p0r cent., was submitted. The Chairman said that he had no doubt they would agree with him that the balance-sheet and report were marvellous productions, and that the shareholders, Li common with the directors, would consider themselves extremely fortunate, especially in view of the un- happy results of other businesses. (Rear, hoar.) He concluded by moving the adoption of toe reprt,a nd the payment of a dividend at the rate of 7 per cent, per annum upon the preference shares, and 30 per cent. per annum noon the ordinary shares on the paid-Up capital. Mr. H. Co4hill seconded the motion, —ln reply to a shareholder, the Chairman said the works at Silvertown were not quite completed, but tilos.> that were finished were in full work, and the whole cf the output was being placed upon the tnarket.—The motion was adopted. Mr. George Jones moved " That the directors, other ' than the managing directors, be paid £5OO for their Fier- ViceS during the half-year ending December 34 1894." Mr. J. R. Darsie seconded the resolution, which/ was carried. On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. C. J. Galloway, the meeting re-elected Messrs. E. Milner, C. M. Rolland, H. Schellhass, and John Crosfield as direc- tors—The Chairman next submitted the recommenda- tion that Mr. Alfred Moritz Mond, of London (son of Mr. Ludwig Mond), be elected as director, remarking that he was a large shareholder, and took a deep interest in the affairs of the company. It was also well, the Chairman added, that limited companies should have as directors men who had a large stake in their welfare. (Rear, hear.)—This was seconded by Mr. Galloway, and carried unanhnously. Messrs. T. W. Read and Co. were re-appointed ac- countants, and the proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to the chairman and the directors.

div.head: PEERS' ECONOMIC BUILDING SOCIETY.
div.p: PEERS' ECONOMIC BUILDING SOCIETY.
ANNUAL MEETING.

--- -- On Tuesday evening the sixth annual meeting of the Peers' Ecoaomie Building Society was held in the office of the secretary, Mr. William Walker, 19, King-st. The chair was occupied by Mr. T. 13ircha1l, J.P., and there was a very good muster of members. The CHAIRMAN, in his opening address, said that the past year had been rather a remarkable one. At the commencement of it they were just coming from under the cloud of the great coal strike of 1893. Throughout the whole of the year,trade never seemed to have rallied, in fact. throuehnut the whole world a state of affairs existed, which he believed to he exceptional, even in his long experience. Trade had been paralysed nowhere more than in the United States. In this country also, the state of things had been very discouraging. There had been a number of withdrawals from the society, but notwith- standing the drawbacks, they had had a very success- ful year. (Applause.) In fact, he was surprised when he looked at the condition of things, and he thoueht it ought to give them confidence to go on. (Hear, hear.) Out of the profits to the credit of the society the direc- tors were able to pay a bonus of is. 61. per share on all paid up shares, which would absorb £34, and also to place £25 to the reserve fund. He considered that the society had every reason to congratulate themselves upon the year's work. Every claim had b 'en satisfied since the society started. He would like to bring before the notice of the members the rule by which with- drawals were paid out of the sums repaid to the society and not eut of the subscriptions. This was only fair to , the other members. He was sure that the directors of , the Riciety did all they could to reduce the workisig expenses. and they would continue to do so. In conclusion, the Chairman read the following annual report :—" The directors have pleasure in sub- mitting their report of the proceedings of the sixth year's working of the society. It will be seen that during the year a further sum of one thousand three hundred pounds has been advanced to members, £4OO of whieh was hallotted and £eoo sold by tender. The latter has produced a substantial profit, as was anticipated in lest year's report, and as appropriations amounting to £4OO have again been purchased during the year, a continued profit may be looked for from this source. The repayments on ' advances have been kept up regularly and the various properties in mortgage to the Society kept in good order and repair. Out of profits standing to the credit of the Society the directors propose to pay a bonus of one shilling and six- pence per share on all paid-up shares, which wild absorb £34, placing £25 to the reserve fund,' as was done last year, and carrying forward the balence to next year's account. The directers feel confident that the reeultof the year's working and the disposal of the profit here indicated will be satisfactory to the members. Tenders may be entimitted at any time for sums raneine from £lOO to £5OO. Messrs. Albinism, )4adshaw, Mounfield, and Hulse retire this year but are eligible far re-election. Mr. Thomas Roberts, the members' auditor, also retiree, but is eligible for re-election." Upon the motion of Mr. HOULT, seconded' by Mr. EVANS, the report and balance sheet were passed unani- mously. The retiring directors, Messrs. Albinson. Bradshaw, Meurifield and Hulse, were all re-elected, Mr. H. J. Longton bearing testimony that they were all hard- working, hard-headed men. The retiring members' auditor, Mr. T. Roberts, was also re-elected. This concluded the business meeting, and an appro- priation was afterwards held.

-- TUE lIAYDOCE PATIENT AT THE PASTEUR INSTITUTE.— Noah Li tiler, the Flaydock collier who is undergoing the Pasteurtreatmers at the Institute, Paris, is reported as doing very well, he not having developed arty bad symptoms. Green, solicitor, St. Helens, who has been con- ducting' s. movement on the part of the tradesmen of I Haydock to get Haydock transferred from Warrington 'to Sr. Helens for county court purposes, on Saturday received the following letter :—" House of Commons, February 15th, 1895. Dear sir,—The Lord Chancellor's secretary informs me that a consolidation of the orders relating to the districts of county courts is now being prepared, and he hopes that.Efaydock will be included in the St. Helens district under the terms of the draft. div.head: SALE OF WORK AT_KARLESTOWN.
div.p: SALE OF WORK AT_KARLESTOWN.

A three day's sale of work fat ttifi purpose of provid- ing funds for reducing the debt of £675 still remaining on the Primitive Methodist Chapel and school, was opened in the schoolroom on Thursday afternoon. The room was crawled at the time of openieg, and on the platform at one end were the Revs. E. R. Davies, F. J. illatt, F. E. Miller, Messrs. T. Molyneux, T. Dreamed, T. Clarke, J. Dickens and T. Austin, jun, The opening ceremony was perfoimed by Mr. Thomas , Molvnenx, previous to which, The Rev. B It. Davies said the chapel was built in the year 1873, costing £GS; in 1884, the school was built at a cost of £B7B. Since that time they had spent in improvements £lBO, so that altogether they had spent on the premises £2,023, and they were valuedat £2,120. The money was borrowed from different sources, bat they had paid off all those who had lent money on the place, and barrowed from their own Chapel Aid Asso- ciation, saving by this means, a per cent. They had howevor had to sign an agreement. that not only had to pay off tho iiiterest, but at least £25 per year of capital. Th?y wanted to do more than that; it would take them ' something like 26 years to pay off the debt at that rate, and he did not think it would satisfy them to go at that slow pace, and that was the reason why they were having that`sale of work. They could have had a sale of work on a small scale, but they thought they could clear off £lOO or so. at one stroke by such a scheme as they inaugurated that day, but he would not venture to prophecy as to the sesult. Re then introduced to them Mr. Molyneux, whom they were pleased to have amongst them. (Hear, hear.) Mr. T. Molyneux, said he had to thank them very sin- cerely for the honour they had conferred upon him in asking him to open the bazaar. It was a very agreeable task, the objects were very fine. They all knew the ob- jects of the sale of work. Mr. Davies had told them the amount of the debt,which there was no doubt was a very great burden, and a great hindrance to good work. Their effort that day was to help to remove that to some ex- tent. Ile had been asked by Mr.flartley to make a propos- al, and it was that Mr. fitrtley and a friend would raise a fourth of the amount remaining at the close of the sale of work, on condition that the Trustees should raise the other three fourths in three years. (Applause.) Iu con- clusion he could only ask them to be as free with their purchases as they could, and he then formally di
leclared

ihe sale open. Mr. T. Clarke moved that the best thanks of these present. and especially of the Trlnteo3, and the Ladies Committee of the sale of work be tendered to Mr. Moly- neux for his presence there that afternoon, and for the many ants of kindness that he done for them and others in the past. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Orrnand seconded, and said he was sure Mr. Moly- , neux had inspired everyone present with the hope that in the near future there was a safe prospect of reducing the debt on tlig place, and if that did not inspire the ladieq to open their purses he did not know what would. —The vote was heartiv accorded. Mr. Molyneux, briefly acknowleeged the compliment, and huslnes3 was then proceeded with. Altogether there were seven stalls, and it will at once be seen that the promenading space was very limited. The stalls were very tastefully laid out, and presented a very pleasing appearance. They were laden with the usual articles which are the necessary adjuncts to a bazaar, the fancy and ornamental predominating. There was an abundance of useful articles, and of clothing for young and old. The decorative art was not neglected, and those with a taste for nick-nacks could have their wants satisfied at a very reasonable cost. The stalls were designated and known by the colour„of their drap- ings, the intermingling of colours lending an., air of en- livenment to the scene. div.head: INDEPENDENT LABOUR PARTY,
div.p: INDEPENDENT LABOUR PARTY,
EARLESTOWN.

On Wednesday evening the Co-operative Hall at Earlestown was crowded with an audience, many of whom were attracted out of pure curiosity, and others in expectation of a scene,the occasion being the invasion cf the ranks of the Independent Labour party, by Mr. G. F. Clarke, to read a paper on "The fallacy of Socialism." The chair was occupied by Mr. S. Scho- field, who was supported by members of the party. Mr. Clarke opened the subject of his paper with a reference to the unsettled state of the working classes of the country, and averred that the most optimistic student of Sociology could not view the condition of things, as they existed, with anything like satisfaction. In sup- port of that he gave a quotation from Benjamin Kidd in his great work on " Social Evolutions," who said "there seemed to be pressing on the country, Social matters of the highest importance, and that it was very probable, before long these would have to receive the attention of the people." Continuing, he said they were met that night for the consideration of one of the many Utopias offered as a panacea for existing evils, and the perfecting of human happiness and for that purpose to examine into the question of Socialism, he divided his paper into five parts, first, the rise and progress of Socialism ; second, the principles of collecjvsm anOn- dividualisin ; third, the question of labour ; fourth, the question of capital ; and lastly, Socialism and the democracy. The earliest developments of what was termed modern Socialism did not carry them hack much further than some 50 or 60 years, at least so far as the name is concerned by which the system was de- signated and understood to-day. Socialistic ideas were promulgated by Philiip of Chalcedon some centuries before Christ. It was thus seen that Socialism had its real basis far back in the ages. It was, however, some 16 years ago since Socialism was definitely organised, the first society to make its appearance being the Social Democratic Federation, being followed by the founda- tion of other Socialistic societies, such as the Guild of St. Matthew and the Fabian Society, all of which pro- mulgated much the same ideas. The Socialism now promulgated seemed to be based upon idea first started by Proudhon, Carl Marx, and Bebel. He gave an outline of What the principles of Socialism were to get at a common under- standing. He said many definitions had been given and quoted the definition of Mr. Bradlaugh which approximated more closely to the generally conceived notion than any other, and which both Socialists and anti-Socialists agreed upon. He gave a definitionTof what he understood by collectivism, meaoing that Socialists intended tbat society should be organised under State direction, and the appointment of State officials to control all the means of Production and possess all the capital in the country and to use it for the benefit of every individual without distinction of position or class. Individualism as the opposite of collectivam was based to a very large extent on a love of self, the Government of all bY all and for all. He proceeded to,at great length ,the various points into which he had divided his arguments, which tended to show that the creed of Socialism was an unworkable fallacy. but want of space provents our entering more fully into the subject of the paper.

div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EA.IILESTO`FI•i.

..,--- (BY AN OCCASIONAL CONTRIBUTOR). I wonder what has become of the Chairman o' .the Gas and Water Committee of the District Council? It is plain I think, to an observant mind that the gas and water are cognisant of the absence of a controlling element, proof being found in the fact that last week one half the town was without water, and it was discovered that instead of taking the proper course of supplying the thirsty inhabit- ants, it went galivanting down the main sewer.- Of course things are apt to get 4 little out of order, if they are allowed to go unattended. Now this week several of the gas lamps haye either turned stupid or gone on the spree; at any rate they have not, on l sundry occasions, been gracious enough to shed a I ray of welcome light at a time when it is most needed, and curious enough this fault has been more noticeable in the ward which the Chairman is supposed to represent. I don't mean to say that the Chairman is responsible for this state of things, but the coincidence is significant. Of course I am not unmindful of the fact that when elected he assured the ratepayers he would do is utmost on their I, behalf. ' '

The death this week of otl bid toirnardan, Mr. Ratcliffe, removes froth bur immediate mto.t a gentleman whore the poor have long considered as their especial benefactor. It is an admitted fact that he Was happiest when looking into cases of disttcss and doing what he possibly could to soften the severe pinches of poverty. Not so very long ago pAople in receipt of parish relief had to tramp, hail, rain, or snow, from Haydock and Earlestown to Newton, to receive their miserable pittance, but Mr. Ratcliffe recognising the hardship such a need- less lourney imposed upon the people,succeeded in getting relief stations established first. at Earles- town and afterwards at Haydock. For other acts, always tending in the same direction, these people have cause to remember him in a kindly and grate- ful manner.

Turning to the other matters, his demise renders vacant the position of district Councillor for Town Hall Ward, and also that of Guardian. I learn that the Tories have already been moving and casting about for a candidate,this plainly showing that the fight for the seat is to be a political one pure and simple. So let it be. I think the Liberals are fully qualified to look after their own interests,!and what, they did before they can do again. Town Hall Ward is not for the Conservatives. It will remain true to its colours,and only send to the Council such as will study the interests of Earlestown in general, and his own ward in particular, from the point of view of a native. At any rate there will be a meeting of Liberals on Monday night, when the candidate will introduced,and I hope every Liberal in the ward will make an effort to be present.

-- In connection with the other vacancy, that of Guardian, it is proposed to run a lady candidate. The Earlestown people, whatever else they may be, are a chivalrous lot, and lam sure they will not for one moment be 80 discourteous as to oppose the candidate of a lady. That being so, her election will be assured, and she will be able to lend con- siderable assistance to the lady who is already a member of the Board of Guardians.

-- The best piece of news I have heard this week,is to the effect that the Liberal Association for tte Newton Division, though young is exceedingly vigorous, and prepared to bite at any moment. It has been repeatedly said by interested people, that Liberalism in Earlestown was practically dead, but I expect that, before another week is over,they will find it has a vigorous existence. Net only have the Liberals got a candidate for the District Coun- cil, but they have secured a strong candidate pre- pared to fight the constituency in the event of a Parliamentary election. Ere many days are pest, this gentleman, will be in the district, and will be introduced to the members of the Liberal Associa- tion. This does not look as 14 Liberalism in the Newton division was dead; it rather savours to me of being very much alive.

Newton lake was crowded with people on Sun- day afternoon-1 mean of course, the ice covering the water forming the lake. To a student of human •character, this WM a golden opportunity, for be could have had a sufficiency of types. I cannot see any harm in promenading on the ace, accompanied by an openly displayed prayer-book, &a., or even to quiet skate, but I do most strongly object to these racing matches, which do not seem to be organised on any 'day but Sunday. But if the Newton folks wink at racing, why object to cricket or tennis on Sunday?
